pages.title: Developing a plugin
pages.description: Scaffold a sandboxed plugin with create-lumen-plugin, run it with hot reload in developer mode, test it in Node with the test kit, and see what it does in the Developer panel.
pages.md:
## Five minutes from nothing to a running plugin

```bash
npx create-lumen-plugin my-plugin
cd my-plugin
npm run dev        # http://127.0.0.1:5199, watches the folder
```

1. In Lumen open **Plugin gallery**, then **Developer mode** at the bottom.
   Keep `http://127.0.0.1:5199` and press **Connect**.
2. Run the command your plugin registers from `⌘K` (in the template: *My plugin*): the side panel shows the word count of the note.
3. Change `main.js` and save. Lumen reloads the plugin by itself, usually
   in well under a second. The panel shows how long the last reload took.

Nothing needs installing: the dev server and the test kit use only Node
(20 or later).

## What is in the folder

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `lumen-plugin.json` | The manifest: id, name, version, and the capabilities the plugin asks for, each with the reason the user sees. |
| `main.js` | The plugin. It runs in the [sandbox](/plugins/sandbox/): only the `lumen` API, no DOM, no network unless asked for. |
| `test/main.test.mjs` | Tests, run with `npm test`. |
| `tools/dev-server.mjs` | The dev server behind `npm run dev`. |
| `tools/testkit.mjs` | The test kit. |

## Developer mode

Developer mode loads the plugin from the dev server instead of the
gallery:

- It connects only to this computer (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`).
- Keep the dev server on port 5199: the app's content security policy
  allows that port on this computer and no other.
- The plugin gets the capabilities its manifest asks for, without the
  permission screen: it is your own code.
- Each version is still run through the [safety scan](/plugins/permissions/),
  and the panel shows its notes. The scan's verdict does not block your own
  plugin here, but the gallery will not list a version that fails.
- On every save the dev server sends a `change` event and Lumen loads the
  manifest and `main.js` again. Changes that arrive during a reload are
  collected into one more reload.

## The Developer panel

While the plugin runs, the panel shows:

- **Reloads**: how many, how long the last one took (from the save to the
  plugin running again), and how long the start took.
- **CPU and memory**: the time spent in the plugin's code, how many runs,
  the longest, and the sandbox's memory.
- **Permissions: asked for and used**: each capability in the manifest,
  how often it was used and refused. A capability that is never used is
  marked: ask only for what you use, because users see the list before
  they install.
- **Last calls**: the plugin's last calls to Lumen, with their time and
  whether they were refused.

## Testing in Node

```js




test("shows the count", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", document: { text: "שלום עולם" } });
  await p.run("show");                       // a command it registered
  assert.equal(p.panel.tree.type, "box");    // the panel it rendered
});

test("needs document:read", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", grants: ["commands", "panel"] });
  await assert.rejects(p.run("show"), { name: "PluginDenied" });
});
```

`loadPlugin` runs `main.js` in a fresh Node `vm` context with a mock of the
`lumen` API. It follows the sandbox's rules: the same method table (a test
in Lumen keeps the two equal), a call without its capability rejects with
`PluginDenied`, and arguments must be JSON. The mock state is `document`
(`text`, `fileName`, `selection`), `vault` (`{"folder/note.md": text}`),
`settings`, `storage` and `fetch` for granted network calls.

You get back what the plugin did: `commands`, `panel`, `rendered`,
`document`, `vault`, `storage`, `notifications`, `clipboard`, `logs`,
`calls` and `denied`. You drive it with `run(id, payload)`,
`emit(name, payload)` (for example `"ui:panel"`), `render(lang, source)`
for a code-block renderer, and `select(from, to)`.

Node is not QuickJS, so test in Lumen too before you publish. Two
differences to keep in mind: QuickJS has no `Intl`, and the sandbox
limits CPU time and memory.

## Examples

The gallery's eight examples are in `public/plugins/examples/`:

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| Word stats | A panel, settings, Hebrew and English counting |
| Callout cards | A code-block renderer, storage |
| Quote of the day | Network access to one origin |
| Table of contents | Reading and writing the note |
| Hebrew date | A renderer and a command, a calendar computed without `Intl` |
| Tasks overview | Reading the whole vault (`vault:read`), a panel with note links |
| Bidi cleaner | Selection or whole note, notifications |
| Text format | A port of an Obsidian plugin (MIT), several commands |

## Publishing

Bump `version` in `lumen-plugin.json` and open a pull request that adds
the folder under `public/plugins/examples/` and a line in its
`index.json`. Run `node scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` first: every version is
scanned, and a version that fails is not listed.

pages.title: Permissions and safety scan
pages.description: Before a sandboxed plugin installs, Lumen shows every permission it asks for in plain language; every version in the registry is scanned, and a version that fails is not shown.
pages.md:
A sandboxed plugin can do nothing until you allow it — see the
[plugin API](/plugins/api/). Two things make that choice informed.

## The install screen

**Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…** opens a screen that lists,
before anything runs, every permission the plugin's manifest asks for:

| Permission | What it lets the plugin do |
|---|---|
| `document:read` | Read the note that is open |
| `document:write` | Change the note that is open (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:read` | Read any note in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:write` | Create and change notes in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `commands` | Add commands to the command palette |
| `panel` | Show a side panel |
| `renderer` | Draw code blocks of its own language in the preview |
| `settings` | Keep its own settings |
| `storage` | Store its own data on this device |
| `clipboard:write` | Copy text to your clipboard (*sensitive*) |
| `notifications` | Show notifications |
| `network:<origin>` | Connect to that one address — and nowhere else (*sensitive*) |

Each line also shows the plugin's own reason (“Why: …”) and the version's
safety scan. **Install and allow** grants exactly what is listed; anything
else the plugin tries is refused by the sandbox, and every network request
appears in the privacy ledger. The code is scanned again right before it
runs, so the card can't describe a different copy.

## The safety scan

Every version in the registry (`public/plugins/examples/index.json`) is
scanned by `scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` into `scan.json`; the gallery shows
each version's card — a grade (A, B, C), a score out of 100, and what the
scan noted. **A version that fails is not shown and cannot be installed.**

The scan reads the code — it never runs it — and fails a version that:

- uses an API whose permission the manifest does not declare (for example
  writes to the note with only `document:read`);
- reaches the network without declaring it, or connects to an origin other
  than the one declared;
- runs code made from text (`eval`, `Function`, string timers), loads more
  code (`import`), or indexes `globalThis` / `lumen` with a computed key;
- is not valid JavaScript, is larger than 512 KB, or has a signature that
  does not verify.

It notes (and lowers the score for) permissions asked for but not used,
indirect use of the API, network addresses built while running, and a
missing or unknown signature.

To check a new version before publishing: add it to `index.json`, then
`node scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` (or `--check` to only verify).

## Reporting a problem

Every card and install screen has **Report a problem**, which opens an issue
with the plugin's id and version filled in.

pages.title: Plugin sandbox and permissions
pages.description: How Lumen runs plugins with no access by default — QuickJS for logic, UI as data, a capability list the user grants.
pages.md:
Lumen runs every plugin with **no access by default**. A plugin gets only
the capabilities you grant it when you install it, and you can revoke them
at any time.

## Where plugin code runs

| Part | Runs in | What it can reach |
|---|---|---|
| Logic (`main`) | [QuickJS](https://github.com/justjake/quickjs-emscripten) (MIT), a separate JavaScript engine compiled to WebAssembly, inside its own Web Worker | Only the `lumen` object. There is no `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `importScripts`, DOM or storage, and no `import` of other modules. |
| Interface (panels, settings, block output) | Lumen itself | The plugin sends a **tree of known elements**: text, heading, paragraph, box, list, button, input, checkbox, select, code, link to a note, divider. There is no `img`, `iframe`, `form`, `style`, `script` or HTML, and no link to a web address. |

The interface is data rather than a sandboxed iframe on purpose. CSP and the
iframe `sandbox` attribute block every channel but one: a frame may always
navigate *itself* (`location = "https://…?" + text`). A tree of known
elements has no such channel.

## Limits

Each plugin has a 32 MB heap and a 512 KB stack. It gets 250 ms of CPU each
time Lumen enters its code (an event, the reply to a call), and its console
is capped at 120 lines a minute. A plugin that goes over a limit, or throws
an error nobody catches, is stopped.

## Capabilities

| Capability | Gives |
|---|---|
| `document:read` / `document:write` | The open note's text and selection / changing it |
| `vault:read` / `vault:write` | Listing and reading notes / writing notes |
| `commands` | Commands in the palette |
| `panel` | A side panel |
| `renderer` | Rendering a code-block language |
| `settings` | A settings section |
| `storage` | Its own key–value storage |
| `clipboard:write` | Copying text |
| `notifications` | Toasts |
| `network:https://exact.origin` | Requests to **that origin only** — https (http only for localhost), no cookies, no redirects, at most 5 MB of response |

Every capability the manifest asks for comes with a reason, which is shown
to you before you grant it. A call without its capability fails inside the
plugin with `PluginDenied` and never reaches Lumen. Lumen checks the grant
a second time on the host side, because the worker is a boundary, not the
policy.

## Network and privacy

Every request a plugin makes appears in the **privacy ledger** under
"Plugin". Under the **local-only** AI policy, plugin requests are blocked
and logged as blocked, even when the plugin has a network grant.

## Manifest (`lumen-plugin.json`)

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "org.example.word-stats",
  "name": "Word stats",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Counts words in the open note",
  "author": "Example",
  "license": "MIT",
  "main": "main.js",
  "capabilities": [
    { "id": "document:read", "reason": "To count the words of the open note" },
    { "id": "commands", "reason": "Adds the “Word stats” command" }
  ]
}
```

pages.md:
Lumen plugins are tiny ESM modules that register custom blocks, commands, and sidebar panels. The host loads them via dynamic `import(url)` so there's no build pipeline to learn — write a function, ship a JS file. ## Sandboxed plugins first :::caution[Being rewritten] Plugins move to an isolated runtime with a permission prompt per capability (plan 11.2); this page is replaced when that lands. `create-lumen-plugin` isn't on npm yet: run it from `packages/create-lumen-plugin` in the repository. ::: `npx create-lumen-plugin` now scaffolds a **sandboxed** plugin: it runs in QuickJS with only the capabilities the user grants, reloads on save in developer mode, and comes with a Node test kit. See [Developing a plugin](/plugins/develop/). New plugins should use it. The rest of this page describes the older unpacked ESM plugins, which run in the page with the permissions below. ## The API Every plugin exports a default `activate(api)` function. The `api` argument has these methods: ```ts interface LumenPluginAPI { registerBlock(lang: string, component: ComponentType<{ source, meta }>): () => void; registerCommand(cmd: { id, label, hint?, icon?, action }): () => void; toast(message: string, kind?: "info" | "success" | "warning" | "error"): void; getDocContent(): string; setDocContent(content: string): void; onDocChange(cb: (content: string) => void): () => void; } ``` `activate` may return a cleanup function that runs when the user disables or unloads the plugin — use it to call the unregister fns the API returned, plus tear down any timers / DOM you created. ## Permissions model `lumen-plugin.json` declares the permissions your plugin needs: | Permission | Granted by default | What it lets you do | | --- | :---: | --- | | `register-block` | ✅ | Add a code-fence renderer | | `register-command` | ✅ | Add palette entries | | `register-panel` | ✅ | Add a right-sidebar panel | | `read-doc` | ✅ | Read the active document | | `write-doc` | ✅ | Mutate the active document | | `workspace-read` | ❌ — prompts user | List + read every note | | `workspace-write` | ❌ — prompts user | Create / overwrite notes | | `network-fetch` | ❌ — prompts user | Make outbound HTTP requests | ## Publishing 1. `npm run build` produces `dist/.js` — single ESM bundle, React left external (Lumen ships its own). 2. Push the dist to npm or any CDN (jsDelivr / unpkg). 3. PR against [`public/plugins/registry.json`](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/public/plugins/registry.json) to list your plugin. Required fields: `id`, `name`, `description`, `version`, `icon`, `url`. ## Example: a custom CSV-with-emoji-header block ```tsx // src/index.ts export default function activate(api: LumenPluginAPI) { return api.registerBlock("emoji-csv", EmojiCsv); } // src/block.tsx export function EmojiCsv({ source }: { source: string }) { const [head, ...rows] = source.split("\n"); const cols = head.split(","); return ( {cols.map((c) => )} {rows.map((r, i) => ( {r.split(",").map((c, j) => )} ))}
{c} 📊
{c}
); } ``` That's the whole plugin. ` ```emoji-csv ` blocks now render with the emoji headers everywhere Lumen renders markdown.

pages.title: Plugin signing keys
pages.description: Decide which publishers' plugins Lumen trusts.
pages.md:
Registry plugins can be signed with an **Ed25519** key. Before installing,
Lumen verifies the signature against the keys you trust, so a compromised
CDN cannot ship modified code.

## Manage trusted keys

Command palette → **Trusted plugin signing keys…**

- **Built-in** keys come from the deployment (`VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS`)
  and cannot be removed from the UI.
- **Your keys** are stored in this browser. Paste the publisher's public key
  and press **Trust key**.

Each key is identified by its **fingerprint** — the SHA-256 of the public
key, in hex. Compare it with the fingerprint the publisher lists on their
website before trusting it.

## Accepted formats

- Base64 SPKI (44 bytes for Ed25519, starts with `MCow`).
- PEM: `-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- … -----END PUBLIC KEY-----`.

Generate a key pair with OpenSSL:

```bash
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out plugin-signing.pem
openssl pkey -in plugin-signing.pem -pubout
```

## Errors

- **Not an Ed25519 public key** — the pasted text is not a 44-byte SPKI
  Ed25519 key (RSA and ECDSA keys are not accepted).
- **Untrusted signer** — the plugin is correctly signed, but by a key you
  have not trusted. Verify the fingerprint, then add the key.

pages.title: Templates
pages.description: Start a note from a template — the built-in ones, the gallery, and the ones you install — and where an installed template lives.
pages.md:
## Start from a template

The command palette lists templates as commands. Pick one and it opens
as a **new, unsaved tab**: it never writes into the note you have open,
and a name that is already taken gets a number (*Meeting notes 2.md*).

## The template gallery

`⌘K → Browse template gallery` opens the gallery: filter by category,
search by name, and **Install** a template. Installing writes it to
`templates/<id>.md` in your vault and adds it to the palette under
**Templates: <name>**. It is an ordinary note, so you can edit it like
any other. With the interface in Hebrew, templates that have a Hebrew
version install in Hebrew.

The gallery's list ships with the app (`public/templates/registry.json`),
so browsing it makes no request to any other site.

## Adding a template to the gallery

See `public/templates/CONTRIBUTING.md` in the repository: one Markdown
file plus an entry in `registry.json` (and a Hebrew file under
`public/templates/he/` when there is one).
---
title: Templates and sample vaults
description: The template gallery, the twenty Israeli templates with their Bases views, placeholders, importing a template from a file, and the three sample vaults.
---

**⌘K → Browse template gallery** opens the gallery. **Install** copies a
template into your workspace as `templates/<id>.md`; from then on it is in
**⌘K → Templates**, and choosing it opens a new, unsaved note from it. The
gallery speaks the UI's language: in Hebrew you get the Hebrew name,
description and body of every template that has one.

## Templates for Israeli use cases

Twenty templates, each in Hebrew and in English:

| Area | Templates |
|---|---|
| Journal | Daily journal (with the Hebrew date), weekly review (Sunday–Thursday) |
| Student | University course (semester, credits), exam (Moed A / B), lecture summary, seminar paper |
| Research | Article to read, research log / experiment |
| Work | Team meeting, one-on-one, project (kanban), task |
| Home | Recipe (meat / dairy / pareve, Shabbat), holiday plan, apartment hunting (₪ rent, arnona, va'ad bayit) |
| Reading and writing | Book I'm reading, book chapter, character |
| Personal | Reserve duty (miluim) log, job application (kanban) |

Every one of them stores its facts as **properties** in the frontmatter, with
English keys (`type`, `status`, `due`…) and values in your language, so the
same note works in Lumen and in Obsidian.

### A Bases view with every template

Each template comes with a companion [`.base` file](/workspace/obsidian-bases/).
Installing the template also writes it to `Bases/` (for example
`Bases/Courses.base`, or `Bases/קורסים.base` in Hebrew): a table, cards or
kanban view of every note with that template's `type`, with column names in
your language. If the file is already there, it is left alone, so your
changes to the view survive a reinstall.

## Placeholders

When a template becomes a note, these are filled in — the same names as
Obsidian's core Templates plugin:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `{{title}}` | the note's name |
| `{{date}}` | today, `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `{{time}}` | now, `HH:mm` |
| `{{hebrewDate}}` | today in the Hebrew calendar, for example `30 Heshvan 5787` |

Anything else in double braces is left as it is.

## Import a template from a file

**⌘K → Import template from file…**, or **Import from file…** at the top of
the gallery, copies a Markdown file you pick into `templates/`. A name that
is taken gets a number (`Recipe.md`, then `Recipe 2.md`), and characters that
can't be in a file name are replaced with spaces. The template is in
**⌘K → Templates** straight away.

## Sample vaults

Three ready-made vaults show the templates, links and Bases views working
together. Each opens from the command palette, in the UI's language, into a
folder of its own:

- **Open sample vault: student** — two courses, lecture summaries and an
  exam with a study plan; views of courses, lectures and exams.
- **Open sample vault: researcher** — a thesis, three articles and two
  experiments; views of the literature, the research log and the papers.
- **Open sample vault: writer** — three chapters and three characters,
  linked to each other; views of the manuscript and the characters.

Like the sample workspace, a sample vault never overwrites anything: running
it again only adds the files that are missing.

pages.description: Clip a page, a selection or your highlights into the vault as Markdown, with its source and date. No server involved.
pages.md:
The Lumen Web Clipper is a Chrome / Edge extension (Manifest V3). It sends
the page to Lumen, and **Lumen** turns it into a note. The extraction
happens in the app, so a clip comes out the same whichever way it arrives.

## Install (developer mode)

1. `chrome://extensions/` → turn on **Developer mode**
2. **Load unpacked** → pick the `extension/` folder of the repository
3. Open the extension's **Settings**: set the address of your Lumen (default
   `http://localhost:5173`), or choose **The Lumen desktop app**.

## Use

- **Save full page**: the toolbar button, or right-click → **Clip to Lumen**.
- **Save selection only**: select text first. Only the selection becomes the note.
- **Highlighter**: toolbar → **Highlighter on/off**, then select passages on
  the page. They are kept per address, marked again when you come back,
  and put at the top of the note (as `==highlight==` quotes) on the next clip.

## How a clip reaches Lumen

| Where Lumen runs | How |
|---|---|
| Browser tab | The extension finds (or opens) the Lumen tab and hands the clip to the page with `postMessage`. The app takes messages only from its own window and origin. |
| Desktop app | A `lumen://clip?…` link. If Lumen is already open, the running window gets it. |

Nothing is uploaded anywhere: there is no clip server.

## What a clip contains

The readable part of the page, found by [Defuddle](https://github.com/kepano/defuddle)
(MIT), with Mozilla Readability (Apache-2.0) as a fallback, and converted to
Markdown by Turndown (MIT):

```yaml
---
title: "The Counterpane"
source: "https://example.com/story"
author: "Ada Pierce"
published: "2026-10-01"
clipped: "2026-10-24"
tags: [clip]
---
```

Links and images point at the original page. Clips go into the library
folder (`Library/`, or `ספרייה/` when Lumen is in Hebrew).

### Templates by site

| Site | Folder | Extra |
|---|---|---|
| Wikipedia (any language) | `Library/Wikipedia` | `license: CC BY-SA 4.0`, `summary` |
| ynet | `Library/ynet` | `summary`, `topics`, `tags: [clip, news]` |
| Haaretz | `Library/Haaretz` | `summary`, `topics`, `tags: [clip, news]` |
| YouTube | `Library/YouTube` | `channel`, `published`, `summary`; the transcript when its panel is open |
| arXiv | `Library/arXiv` | `authors`, `arxiv`, `published`, `pdf`, `contribution`; the abstract |
| GitHub repositories | `Library/GitHub` | `description`, `purpose` |
| Pages marked as a schema.org `Recipe` | `Library/Recipes` | `tags: [clip, recipe]` |

A template is picked by its triggers: an address prefix, a `/regular expression/`
or `schema:@Type`. The first match wins.

Besides `{{title}}`, `{{url}}`, `{{content}}` and the rest, a template can read
the page with `{{meta:name}}` (a `<meta>` tag, by name, property or itemprop;
several tags of one name are joined) and `{{selector:css}}` (the text of the
elements a CSS selector picks).

## Interpreter: fields a local model fills in

A template can ask questions about the page: `{{"a one-sentence summary"}}`,
`{{"three key topics"|lower}}`. When a clip uses such a template, Lumen asks a
**model on your own device** — Ollama on this computer or your local network,
or the in-browser model if it is already loaded — and writes the answers into
the note. There is no cloud route: under any AI policy, the interpreter never
sends a page to an AI provider. With no local model running, those fields are
left out and the clip is saved as usual.

- The model reads only what the template points at (its `context` selectors:
  the abstract on arXiv, the lead section on Wikipedia, the transcript on
  YouTube), cut to about 6 000 characters, so a small model's window is
  enough. No `OLLAMA_ORIGINS` or context-size setting is needed in the
  desktop app.
- All questions of a template go in one request.
- The page text passes the prompt-injection guard before the model sees it,
  marked as outside data, and every answer is checked again before it is
  written into the note.

## Safety

A clip is outside content. Its `source:` marks the note as untrusted for the
AI agents (plan 2.7). Before the
note is saved, hidden text (zero-width characters, invisible tag characters,
hidden HTML) and instruction-like passages ("ignore previous instructions…")
are removed or visibly marked, with a warning at the top of the note.

## Accuracy

On the clipper golden set (plan 7.10: 20 pages with ads, cookie banners,
share bars, comments and footers around a public-domain article), the clip
must have the exact title, every paragraph in order and no noise on at least
90 % of pages. This is checked on every change (`clipperGolden.test.ts`).

pages.description: Where to talk about Lumen, how the Hebrew beta works, how to join, and the code of conduct.
pages.md:
Lumen is built in the open, in Hebrew and English.

## The beta

- **Joining:** open a discussion in the **Beta** category of the project's
  GitHub Discussions. It's a short form, and you need a GitHub account.
  The beta page (`/beta.html`) explains it all and sends nothing by itself.
- **What you get:** new features before everyone else. They ship behind
  feature flags in beta builds first.
- **What we ask:** use Lumen for real writing a few times a week, and tell
  us what got in the way, in **Beta feedback**.
- **The weekly survey:** a short, voluntary poll, *how many days this week
  did you open Lumen?* It is the only way we count testers. Lumen has no
  analytics and doesn't count you.
- **Keep a backup:** *Export the whole vault* now and then. It's a beta.

## Where to talk

| For | Where |
|---|---|
| Beta feedback: bugs, ideas, Hebrew and RTL problems | Discussions → *Beta feedback* |
| A confirmed bug or a concrete feature | GitHub Issues |
| Questions, show and tell | Discussions → *Q&A*, *Show and tell* |
| Security problems | privately, as in `SECURITY.md` |

Hebrew or English, whichever you prefer.

## The code of conduct

The project follows the
[Contributor Covenant 2.1](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html).
The repository has it in English (`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`) and in Hebrew
(`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.he.md`). In short:

- assume good intent;
- criticise the work, not the person;
- no harassment, no personal attacks, no sharing others' private
  information.

Reports go privately to the maintainers, as described in `COMMUNITY.md`,
and are kept confidential.

## How Lumen compares

The [comparison page](/project/compare/) puts Lumen next to Obsidian, Notion
and Google Docs on five points, with a source for every claim and a list of
what Lumen still lacks.

pages.title: Lumen, Obsidian, Notion and Google Docs
pages.description: An honest comparison for people who write in Hebrew: what each one does, with a source for every claim, and what Lumen still lacks.
pages.md:
Each one is good at something. This page says what each does on five points that matter when you write in Hebrew, and every claim links to where it can be checked. Claims about the other products come from their own pages.

## Price

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Free. In the browser there is nothing to install, and notes stay in the browser's private storage. | [Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/) · <https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/LICENSE> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Free, for personal use and, since February 2025, for work too. Sync is a paid add-on ($4 a month, billed yearly). | <https://obsidian.md/blog/free-for-work/> · <https://obsidian.md/pricing.html> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Notion** | A free plan and paid plans; see Notion's pricing page. | <https://www.notion.com/pricing> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Google Docs** | Free with a Google account; Google Workspace plans for organisations. | <https://workspace.google.com/pricing> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## Hebrew and right-to-left

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Interface in Hebrew with a mirrored layout; direction per line; search that ignores niqqud and Hebrew prefixes. | [Lumen docs](/editor/hebrew/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Since version 1.6: a mirrored interface for right-to-left languages, Hebrew among them, and notes in RTL, LTR or both. | <https://docs.obsidian.md/Plugins/User+interface/Right-to-left> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Notion** | Interface in Hebrew, mirrored in the desktop and mobile apps; text direction detected in most blocks, but not in simple tables. | <https://www.notion.com/help/change-your-language> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Google Docs** | Right-to-left controls turn on for documents with RTL text; paragraph direction and table column order can be set. | <https://support.google.com/docs/answer/65166> (Checked 2026-11-10) |

## Working offline

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | The installed web app opens and works without a network; notes are stored on the device. | [Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Notes are files in a folder on the device, so they open without a network. | <https://help.obsidian.md/data-storage> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Notion** | Since August 2025, offline in the desktop and mobile apps (not the browser): downloaded pages, plus Recents and Favorites on Plus, Business and Enterprise. | <https://www.notion.com/releases/2025-08-19> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Google Docs** | Offline editing in Chrome or Edge with the Google Docs Offline extension, turned on per account. | <https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6388102> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## Markdown files

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Every note is a plain Markdown file; the whole vault exports as a .zip or a folder. | [Lumen docs](/workspace/export-import/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Notes are Markdown files. | <https://help.obsidian.md/data-storage> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Notion** | Pages live in Notion's database; they can be exported as Markdown. | <https://www.notion.com/help/export-your-content> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Google Docs** | Since July 2024, import Markdown as a Doc and export a Doc as Markdown. | <https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/07/import-and-export-markdown-in-google-docs.html> (Checked 2026-11-10) |

## Source code

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Open source under the MIT licence. | <https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/LICENSE> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | The app's source code is not published. | <https://obsidian.md/license> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Notion** | Proprietary. | <https://www.notion.com/terms> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Google Docs** | Proprietary. | <https://policies.google.com/terms> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## What Lumen still lacks

- No sync service of its own yet: between devices, keep the vault in a folder you already sync, or export and import. ([Lumen docs](/workspace/export-import/))
- Real-time co-editing is peer to peer and young; Google Docs and Notion are far ahead for teams. ([Lumen docs](/collab/webrtc/))
- Far fewer plugins and templates than Obsidian's community. ([Lumen docs](/plugins/sdk/))
- The phone apps are not in the App Store or Google Play yet; on a phone Lumen runs in the browser or as an installed web app. ([Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/))
- It is a beta: expect rough edges, and keep a backup (Export the whole vault). ([Lumen docs](/workspace/export-import/))

This page is generated from `launch/comparison.json` by `node scripts/launch-check.mjs --write`. To correct a claim, change the JSON with a source, and the page follows.

pages.title: Issue triage
pages.description: How new GitHub issues are labelled, checked for duplicates and linked to the plan within 24 hours.
pages.md:
Every new issue on [talstilkol/lumen-md](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/issues)
is looked at by a script within 24 hours, and a person reads it as well. The
script is `scripts/issue-triage.mjs`; the workflow `.github/workflows/issue-triage.yml`
runs it when an issue is opened or reopened and once a day at 06:23 UTC.

## What an issue gets

| What | When | Label |
|---|---|---|
| Kind | from words in the title and body (English and Hebrew) | `bug`, `enhancement`, `question` or `documentation` |
| Area | up to two, the ones whose words appear most | `area:editor`, `area:hebrew`, `area:ai`, `area:storage`, … |
| Possible duplicate | another issue, open or closed, has a near-identical title | `duplicate?` |
| Reproduction request | a bug with no steps, browser or version | `needs-repro` |
| Plan task | a task number in the text (for example `4.5`), else the plan task whose title shares the most words | — (in the comment) |
| Done | always | `triaged` |

When there is something to say (a possible duplicate, missing steps, a plan
task) the script leaves **one** comment, in English and Hebrew. It finds its
own comment again by a hidden marker, so a rerun never comments twice. Labels
that do not exist yet are created.

## What it does not do

- It never closes, assigns or edits an issue, and never removes a label.
- Issue text is only matched against word lists: it is not executed and not
  sent anywhere. The script talks to GitHub's REST API through `gh` with the
  workflow's own token (`issues: write`) and nothing else.

## The daily report

The daily run writes a report — the issues of the last 24 hours with the labels,
duplicate and plan task each got — to the job summary and as the artifact
`reports-issue-triage`. Any open issue older than 24 hours that still has no
`triaged` label is listed and **fails the run**, so the 24-hour promise is
checked every day.

## Running it yourself

```bash
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs                 # dry run: prints what it would do
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs --apply         # writes labels and comments
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs --json out.json # the report as JSON too
```

A dry run needs only a logged-in `gh`; `--apply` needs write access to issues.

pages.title: Public roadmap
pages.description: The roadmap page at /roadmap — generated from plan/plan.json, titles and status only, and checked in CI so it cannot drift.
pages.md:
Every Lumen deployment serves an open roadmap at `/roadmap.html` (and at
`/roadmap` on Cloudflare Pages, Netlify and the Docker image). The status bar's
**Roadmap** link opens it.

## Where it comes from

The page is the third output of `npm run plan`, next to the board in
`MASTER_PLAN.md` and `plan/board.html`. All three are rendered from one file,
`plan/plan.json`, and `npm run plan:check` fails CI when any of them differs
from it. So the roadmap changes in the same commit as the plan, every time.

## What it shows — and what it does not

| Shown | Not shown |
|---|---|
| every phase, with its number and title | the steps of a task and its acceptance line |
| every task's number and title | estimates, dates and the schedule |
| its state: **done** (✅), **in progress** (⏳) or **planned** | branches, PR numbers and the owner's items (phase 15) |
| the counts and a progress bar | anything from issues or notes |

The full plan, with every measured acceptance criterion, is in the repository.

## How it renders

`public/roadmap.html` carries the data as a JSON block; `public/roadmap.js`
builds the cards with `textContent`. The script is external because the app's
Content-Security-Policy allows no inline script, and it needs no Trusted Types
policy because it never writes HTML. The page is Hebrew and right-to-left,
laid out with logical CSS properties.

## Updating it

```bash
npm run plan        # rewrites MASTER_PLAN.md's board, plan/board.html and public/roadmap.html
npm run plan:check  # what CI runs: exit 1 when any of them is out of date
```

pages.title: Usability tests with Hebrew speakers
pages.description: How Lumen is tested with people who write in Hebrew — the ten tasks, SUS, the consent-first session recorder that keeps no note text, and the analysis.
pages.md:
The project measures a lot, and sessions with real people measure what
nothing else does: whether someone who writes in Hebrew can do the common
things without help. The kit is in
[`research/usability/`](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/tree/main/research/usability)
and everything in it is in Hebrew, the participants' language.

## The study

- **Who:** 8 participants per round, at least 5: two students, two
  researchers, two writers and two developers. All work in Hebrew and are new
  to Lumen.
- **What:** ten tasks, one at a time, thinking aloud, with no help from the
  moderator:
  1. a new note;
  2. a checklist;
  3. linking notes;
  4. search;
  5. tags;
  6. Hebrew and English on one line;
  7. a table;
  8. export to PDF;
  9. restoring from the trash;
  10. the daily note.
- **Measured:**
  - success, success without help, and time, per task;
  - the ease question (SEQ, 1–7) after each task;
  - the System Usability Scale (SUS, 0–100) at the end.
- **Rounds:** the ten most severe issues from round 1 become plan tasks.
  Round 2, with new participants, checks the fixes. The goal is a mean SUS
  of at least 80, at least 90% unaided success, and all ten severe issues
  closed. The study is repeated before every major release.

## The session recorder

Command palette → **Usability study (moderator)…** opens the moderator's
panel. It is off until then, and it records nothing until the participant
has signed the consent form and the moderator ticks the box.

| Recorded | Never recorded |
|---|---|
| when each task started and ended, and its outcome | anything typed into notes, note or file names |
| controls clicked, by role and by the app's own label | a label that isn't one of the app's UI strings (it becomes `[label]`) |
| commands run, by id | the participant's name (a code: P1, P2, …) |
| how many keys were pressed, and modifier shortcuts | which characters were typed |
| the SEQ and SUS answers, and the moderator's observation codes | free-text notes (the moderator keeps those on paper) |

- **Local:** the data stays in the browser and leaves only as the JSON file
  the moderator saves. The recorder makes no request.
- **Deletion:** *Delete session data* removes it, and anything left on the
  device is deleted after 30 days. The consent form promises that session
  files are deleted once the round's analysis is written.

## The analysis

`node scripts/usability-analyze.mjs <folder> --round 1` turns a round's
session files into a report:

- per task: success, success without help, median time, SEQ, errors and
  help opened;
- SUS per participant, and the mean with a 95% confidence interval.

With `--round 2 --findings …` it also checks the plan's acceptance criteria
against the findings file. With 5–8 people the numbers show a direction,
not statistical significance.

The Hebrew SUS wording is the study's own translation, not a validated one.
It compares rounds with each other; comparisons with published SUS norms
are approximate.

pages.title: Allowed image hosts
pages.description: See which sites may always load images in your notes, and revoke one or all of them.
pages.md:
An image from another site tells that site you opened the note. So Lumen
doesn't load it until you say so: the preview shows a placeholder with
**Load** (this image, until you reload the page) and **Always allow**
(every image from that site, in this browser).

## The list, and revoking

Command palette → **Privacy: allowed image hosts…** lists every site you
chose **Always allow** for.

- **Revoke** next to a site: its images wait for you again, at once — the
  preview shows the placeholder and nothing more is requested from that
  site. Images from it you loaded once with **Load** in this session are
  blocked again too.
- **Revoke all** does it for every site.

The list is kept in this browser (localStorage), not in your notes or your
vault, so another browser or device has its own.

The desktop app loads no images from other sites at all; there is nothing
to allow there.

pages.title: Monitoring and web vitals
pages.description: Error reports are off by default and sent only with your consent; web vitals never leave your device.
pages.md:
Lumen measures how fast it is on your device, and can send crash reports
to an error tracker, but only after you turn them on. Both work the same
way in every build.

## Web vitals: measured here, never sent

Lumen measures five page-speed metrics with the browser's
`PerformanceObserver`:

| Metric | What it is | Good |
|---|---|---|
| LCP | Largest Contentful Paint: when the largest visible element appears | ≤ 2.5 s |
| FCP | First Contentful Paint: when the first content appears | ≤ 1.8 s |
| TTFB | Time to First Byte: when the server's first response byte arrives | ≤ 800 ms |
| INP | Interaction to Next Paint: the slowest interaction this session | ≤ 200 ms |
| CLS | Cumulative Layout Shift: how much the layout jumps without your input | ≤ 0.1 |

The values stay in memory on your device. Open them with **Runtime
metrics** in the status bar, or from the command palette. They are never
sent, even when error reports are on. A sample stores no page address.

## Error reports: off by default

Lumen sends error reports only when **both** of these are true:

1. **You turned them on.** Click the **Telemetry** pill in the status bar.
   It is off in a fresh install. Click it again to turn reports off.
   Turning them off takes effect at once, even for an error that is
   already being reported.
2. **The build names an error tracker** in `VITE_SENTRY_DSN`. This can be
   Sentry or a self-hosted GlitchTip, which speaks the same protocol.

If either one is missing, the Sentry SDK is never downloaded and no
request is made. The default build has no DSN, so it makes no monitoring
requests at all. An e2e test (`e2e/monitoring.spec.ts`) checks this.

### What a report contains

Each report is rebuilt from a short allowlist before it leaves the browser:

- the error's class name, such as `TypeError`;
- the script file names, functions and line numbers of the stack trace;
- the app's release and environment, and the SDK's name and version.

The error **message is never sent**. A message can contain a title or a
line of a note without quotes ("Failed to save Quarterly plan"), and no
filter can reliably tell that apart from the app's own words. The stack
trace shows where the error happened, and that is enough to find it.

A report never includes:

- the error message, or any text logged with it;
- the page address;
- breadcrumbs, such as clicks, console lines and requests;
- user or IP data (`infer_ip: never`);
- tags, extra data or contexts.

There is no session replay, no performance tracing and no session
tracking.

### Every report is in the privacy ledger

Error reports go through the privacy ledger (command palette → **Privacy
ledger**) like every other request that leaves the device. Each one is listed under its own
category: "Error report — only with your consent, content removed". The
ledger shows where the report went, its size and its status. Under the
**local-only** AI policy, reports are refused before they leave, and each
refusal is listed as blocked.

## For operators: setting the DSN

Set the DSN at build time:

```bash
VITE_SENTRY_DSN=https://<public-key>@o123.ingest.sentry.io/4567 npm run build
# Docker: docker build --build-arg VITE_SENTRY_DSN=… .
```

**A DSN is not a secret.** Sentry designs it to be public: it ships in
every page that uses Sentry, and it only lets a client *submit* events
to one project. It can't read data. So a build-time `VITE_*` variable is
the right place for it, and secret scanners may ignore it.

The DSN's host is added to the CSP `connect-src` **automatically at build
time**, through the same mechanism as the other deployment endpoints
(`src/build/cspEndpoints.ts`). That covers the `index.html` meta tag,
`dist/_headers` and the nginx image. On **Vercel**, `vercel.ts` adds the
same origin to the header it serves, from the project's `VITE_SENTRY_DSN`
environment variable. No error-tracker host or wildcard is in the
checked-in policies.

## בעברית

- **מדדי ביצועים (Web Vitals)** נמדדים במכשיר שלך ולא נשלחים לשום מקום.
  אפשר לראות אותם בחלון "מדדי ריצה" בשורת המצב.
- **דוחות שגיאה כבויים כברירת מחדל.** הם נשלחים רק אם הפעלת אותם בכפתור
  "טלמטריה" בשורת המצב, **וגם** הבנייה כוללת כתובת DSN של שירות מעקב.
- הדוח כולל רק את סוג השגיאה ואת מיקומה בקוד. הודעת השגיאה, תוכן הפתקים,
  הכותרות והנתיבים לא נשלחים. אין הקלטת סשן ואין מידע מזהה.
- כל דוח מופיע ביומן הפרטיות. במדיניות "מקומי בלבד" הדוחות נחסמים.

pages.title: Mutation testing
pages.description: How Lumen checks that the tests of its security-critical code, such as encryption, the keyring, sync merges and the privacy ledger, really catch bugs.
pages.md:
Coverage tells you which lines ran, not whether a test would notice if they
were wrong. Mutation testing checks that. It plants small bugs in the code,
one at a time, and runs the tests each time. A test suite that still passes
with a bug in place has missed it.

## What is tested

The pure modules whose bugs would hurt most:

- **Encryption primitives:** ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2b, scrypt and Argon2id.
- **age** file encryption, and the **keyring** that holds the vault keys and
  devices.
- The **sync engine**: conflict merging, the manifest and blob headers.
- The **privacy ledger**, which records and blocks anything that would leave
  the device.
- The **secret store** (API keys and tokens: encrypted in the browser, or in
  the OS keychain on desktop), the **raw-HTML sanitizer** of the preview,
  Hebrew **text matching**, file **encryption**, **ZIP** import limits, and
  the **agent runtime**.

The list is in `scripts/mutation/targets.json`.

## The bugs it plants

| Kind | Example |
|---|---|
| Operators | `+` ↔ `-`, `<` ↔ `<=`, `===` ↔ `!==`, `&&` ↔ `\|\|`, `<<` ↔ `>>`, `^` → `&` |
| Constants | `n` → `n + 1` (`1` → `0`) |
| Booleans | `true` ↔ `false` |
| Negation | `!x` → `x` |
| Conditions | `if (c)` → `if (!(c))` |

Only code is mutated, never types, imports or comments. A mutant that
doesn't parse is left out. A mutant counts as **caught** when a test that
passes on the real code fails, when the run crashes, or when it hangs.

## Running it

```sh
npm run test:mutation                          # all modules, fails under 70%
node scripts/mutation/run.mjs --module keyring # one module
node scripts/mutation/run.mjs --max 200        # a bigger sample per module
```

The report, with the score per module and every surviving mutant's line, is
written to `reports/mutation/`. The plan's target is a score of at least
70% per module. A mutant that survives in a security module should get a
test that catches it.

pages.title: A privacy report you can prove
pages.description: Export the privacy ledger as a signed report, check it with a script, and see the results of the outside audit for every version.
pages.md:
"Private" is a claim. Lumen lets you check it. The privacy ledger lists
every network request Lumen's features make. You can export it as a
**signed report**, check that report with a script, and compare it with
what an **outside network analyzer** saw during the same run.

## Export the report

⌘K → *Privacy ledger…* → **Export signed report**. The file covers this
session, from when the tab opened. For each request it says:

| | |
|---|---|
| Who | Which feature (its category and reason: "Anthropic (Claude)", "Model download", …) |
| When | The time |
| Where | The host |
| How much | Bytes sent and received, and whether it was allowed or blocked |

The summary (requests, how many left the device and to which hosts, bytes)
is computed from those entries. The file holds no prompt, note or header.

It is signed in the browser with **Ed25519**, using a key made on this device
the first time you export. The private half stays in IndexedDB and can't be
exported. The signature uses the minisign format, so both the script below
and the `minisign` tool can verify it.

## Check a report

```sh
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs lumen-privacy-report-….json
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --local-only          # also: nothing left the device
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --pub device.pub      # pin the signing key
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --extract out/        # then: minisign -Vm out/report.json -p out/report.pub
```

The script checks the signature and the trusted comment (which names the
report's SHA-256), and that the report is in its canonical form. It checks
the shape of every entry: times inside the session and in order,
`leftDevice` following the ledger's rule. It then **works the summary out
again** and refuses a report whose summary disagrees with its entries.
Without `--pub`, it proves the file hasn't changed since it was signed. With
`--pub`, it also proves which device signed it.

## Audit mode

The ledger normally lists AI traffic. In **audit mode**
(`localStorage["lumen.privacy.audit"] = "1"`) it also lists every other
request that leaves the device and the LAN, as *Other request*. Those are
listed but never blocked. The app is then run through an outside analyzer:

```sh
node scripts/privacy/audit.mjs --sign ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.key --publish
```

1. **mitmproxy** (`mitmdump`, 10.1 or newer) records every request,
   including the app's own requests to the dev server, which proves it was
   in the path.
2. `e2e/privacy-audit.spec.ts` runs the journey under the **local-only**
   policy with cloud keys set to tempt every fallback: the views, an export,
   the AI commands, and a hand-made cloud request (which is blocked). It then
   exports the signed report and keeps Playwright's own request log.
3. The script verifies the report and compares it with **both** observers.
   The audit passes only when each observer saw traffic, nothing it saw
   leaving is missing from the report, nothing the report lists is missing
   from the wire, and **0 requests are non-local**.
4. `audit.json` is signed with the [release key](/security/supply-chain/)
   and published below.

## Results per version

Every version since the first audit has its row. `publish.mjs --check`
fails when a released version (in `CHANGELOG.md`) has no audit file in
`security/privacy-audits/`.

<!-- audits:start -->
_No audit published yet: the first runs with the first release after this page._
<!-- audits:end -->

## Store privacy labels

`store/privacy-labels.json` is the source for the App Store's *App Privacy*
answers and Google Play's *Data safety* form:

- **Data not collected.** With default settings nothing leaves the device,
  which is what the local-only audit shows.
- **Crash data, only on one condition:** the build has a crash-reporting key
  and the user hasn't opted out. It isn't linked to the user and isn't used
  for tracking.
- Every optional feature that can send something, mapped to its category in
  the ledger.

A test keeps the labels in step with the ledger's categories, the crash
reporter and the published audits.

pages.title: Secret scan of the build
pages.description: Why no secret may be a VITE_* variable, the gate that fails a build that sets one, and the scan of the live deployments.
pages.md:
Vite copies the value of every `VITE_*` variable the app reads into the
public JavaScript. Anyone who opens the site can read it. So a token, an
API key or a password must never be a `VITE_*` variable. Lumen enforces
this in three places.

| Where | What it checks | What fails |
|---|---|---|
| The build (`vite build`) | Every `VITE_*` variable set in the environment or in an `.env` file | A name not on `security/vite-env-allowlist.json` |
| The Vercel preview gate (`npm run secrets:dist`) | Every file in `dist/` | A token shape, or an inlined `VITE_*` value not on the allowlist |
| The live scan (`npm run secrets:scan-live`) | Production, the 3 newest previews, and the `VITE_*` names set in Vercel | The same, plus a `VITE_*` name in Vercel that is not on the allowlist |

The code rules in `npm run hygiene` keep secret-named reads (`…TOKEN`,
`…SECRET`, `…KEY`) and reads of `import.meta.env` as a whole object out of
`src/`. Before #243 such a whole-object read put **every** `VITE_*`
variable of the build into the bundle, even ones the app never used. The
allowlist gate covers that case too: a build cannot set a name that is not
listed.

## The allowlist

`security/vite-env-allowlist.json` lists each name a build may set, with
the reason it is public: a worker URL, an OAuth client id, a price id, a
public key. Names that start with `VITE_VERCEL_` are Vercel's system
variables (the deployment id, the git branch and commit). They are not
secrets, and the app reads none of them. A value that starts with
`ci-canary-` is a test canary and is allowed under any name.

To add a variable, add its name and the reason it is public. If it is a
secret, it does not belong here: keep it in the secret store
(`src/lib/secretStore.ts`) or on the server.

## What the scan looks for

- **Secret** (the scan fails): OpenAI and Anthropic keys (`sk-`), GitHub
  tokens (`ghp_`, `github_pat_` …), Google API keys (`AIza`), AWS access
  keys, Stripe live keys, Slack tokens, private-key bodies, JWTs other
  than a public anon key, and inlined `VITE_*` values not on the allowlist.
- **For review** (listed only): hex strings of 32 or more characters, and
  anon JWTs. Content hashes and embed ids look the same.

A report never shows a whole value. It shows the first 4 characters and
the length.

## Running it

```bash
npm run secrets:self-test        # plants a token of each kind in a temporary build and finds it
npm run secrets:dist             # scans dist/ after npm run build
VERCEL_TOKEN=… VERCEL_PROJECT_ID=prj_… VERCEL_TEAM_ID=team_… \
  npm run secrets:scan-live -- --report scan.md
node scripts/secrets-scan-live.mjs --url https://lumen-md.vercel.app
```

The live scan reads the **names** of the project's environment variables
from the Vercel API. It never asks for a value to be decrypted. For a
protected preview, set `VERCEL_AUTOMATION_BYPASS_SECRET`.

## If a secret was a VITE_* variable (15.18)

1. Treat it as public. Any build that ran while it was set may have put it
   in the bundle, and old deployments stay online.
2. Revoke it with the provider and create a new one.
3. Delete the `VITE_*` variable in Vercel (and in Netlify or CI, if used).
4. Put the new value where it belongs: the secret store for a user's key,
   or a server-side secret for a worker.
5. Run `npm run secrets:scan-live` and keep the report.

If no secret was ever set as `VITE_*`, record that, and 15.18 is done.

pages.title: Supply chain
pages.description: Fuzzed decoders, a reproducible build, an SBOM and offline-signed checksums for every release — and how anyone can check them.
pages.md:
The [threat model](/security/threat-model/) assumes the code you run is the
code that was released. Four checks make that verifiable.

## 1. The decoders are fuzzed

Everything Lumen reads from a file, a link, the clipboard or a plugin goes
through a decoder: the Markdown pipeline, front matter, BibTeX, JSON and
JSONL (Code Doctor, Insights), URLs (sanitizer, embeds, the CSP check), text
direction — and `.base`, `.excalidraw`, PDF annotations and plugin
manifests as those land.

```bash
npm run fuzz                                    # 1,000,000 inputs per decoder
node scripts/fuzz/run.mjs --target bibtex --runs 50000
node scripts/fuzz/run.mjs --target bibtex --seed 1 --from 4242 --runs 1   # replay one input
```

Inputs are built from each format's own pieces (with Hebrew, Arabic, bidi
controls, emoji and lone surrogates), then cut, repeated and nested
thousands deep. Each decoder runs in its own worker: an exception it does
not document is a **crash**; one input running over a second is a **hang** —
the worker is stopped and the run continues. Failing inputs are saved to
`fuzz-findings/` with the command that replays them. The pass criterion is
0 crashes and 0 inputs over 1 s.

`--engine fast-check` runs the same decoders through
[fast-check](https://fast-check.dev) (with shrinking) once it is installed.

**Pathological Markdown (plan W4.16).** The first run found seven inputs
(8–14 KB) that took 0.5–2.8 s to render: thousands of `[` or `]` in one
paragraph, or lists nested 231 levels deep, make the parser's work grow with
the square of the text. A note like that would freeze the editor. Now a
block (the text between blank lines) with more than 256 brackets or more
than 32 nesting levels is shown as raw text, in a code block, exactly as
written (`src/renderer/boundMarkdown.ts`). Every real note stays far inside
both bounds and renders as before. The live preview also shows a block as
raw text once its render took more than 200 ms. The seven inputs are pinned
in `src/__tests__/markdownSlowInputs.test.ts` (each under 50 ms).

## 2. The build is reproducible

```bash
npm run repro
```

builds the same commit twice from clean (with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` set to
the commit time) and compares the SHA-256 of every file in `dist/`. Any
difference is listed by file.

A release build has no source maps (plan 11.5), and the check fails if one
appears, so there is no map that could differ between two builds. Maps are
for a local investigation only (`LUMEN_SOURCEMAP=1`):
`node scripts/supply-chain/repro-check.mjs --sourcemap` builds with them and
says which fields of each differing map differ.

## 3. Every release has an SBOM

```bash
npm run sbom          # → release/sbom.cdx.json
```

A CycloneDX 1.5 list of every npm package (`package-lock.json`) and every
Rust crate (`src-tauri/Cargo.lock`): version, package URL, the lockfile's
hash and the licence. Same lockfiles, same bytes.

## 4. Every release is signed — offline

The signing key belongs to the release owner and never enters a CI system.

**Once** (on the owner's machine):

```bash
LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE=… node scripts/supply-chain/keys.mjs --out ~/.lumen-release
cp ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.pub security/release-key.pub   # commit this file only
```

Keep `lumen-release.key` and its passphrase offline (a password manager
and a second offline copy). Old releases stay verifiable with the old
public key if the key is ever replaced.

**Each release:**

```bash
npm run repro && npm run build
LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE=… npm run release:sign -- --key ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.key \
  --artifact <each desktop / mobile file>
```

This writes `release/SHA256SUMS` (every file of `dist/` and each artifact),
`release/sbom.cdx.json` and a minisign signature of each, then checks the
result. Upload the four files with the release.

**Anyone can check a release:**

```bash
npm run release:verify                      # signatures + every file against SHA256SUMS
# or with the standard tools:
minisign -Vm SHA256SUMS -P <public key from security/release-key.pub>
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
```

The signatures are standard minisign (Ed25519 over BLAKE2b-512), made with
Node's own crypto — no extra package.

## OpenSSF Best Practices

The [OpenSSF Best Practices badge](https://www.bestpractices.dev) is
claimed by the project owner. What it asks for, and where it is:

| Criterion | Here |
|---|---|
| Public repo, licence, contribution and security-report docs | `LICENSE`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md` |
| Version-controlled, unique version per release, release notes | git tags, `CHANGELOG.md`, `RELEASE.md` |
| Automated tests and a test policy for new code | vitest + Playwright; every task's Definition of done |
| Static analysis and dependency scanning | ESLint, CodeQL, `npm audit`, `cargo audit`, gitleaks (`.github/workflows/security.yml`) |
| Dynamic analysis (fuzzing) | `npm run fuzz` |
| Signed releases, reproducible build | `npm run release:sign` / `release:verify`, `npm run repro` |
| A vulnerability report process with response times | `SECURITY.md` (acknowledged within 48 h, a fix timeline within 5 business days, 90-day disclosure) |

pages.description: window.__lumen.agentReview exists only in development and tests.
pages.md:
The end-to-end tests drive a few app functions through `window.__lumen`.
One of them, `window.__lumen.agentReview`, stages a change for the
[agent review screen](/ai/agents/) the way an agent's write tool does. A
page script that could call it could put changes in front of you that no
agent proposed, so it is **not part of the app you install**.

## Where it exists

| Build | `window.__lumen.agentReview` |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` (Vite dev server) | yes |
| `npx vitest` (unit tests) | yes |
| `VITE_LUMEN_TEST_SURFACE=1 npm run build` (the e2e-prod job only) | yes |
| `npm run build` (every release, the PWA, desktop and mobile) | **no** — the code is removed from the bundle |

The release build replaces `import.meta.env.DEV` and
`VITE_LUMEN_TEST_SURFACE` with constants, so the surface and the function
behind it are dropped when the bundle is minified.

## Checking a build

```sh
npm run build
npm run check:test-surface
```

`check:test-surface` reads every JavaScript file under `dist/` and fails if
one still sets or reads `.agentReview` (the translation keys such as
`agentReview.title` are text and do not count). CI runs it after the
production build.

pages.title: Threat model
pages.description: What Lumen protects, from whom, at each of its boundaries — vault, sync, sharing, plugins, agents and the web clipper — and where each defence is tested.
pages.md:
Privacy is Lumen's central claim, so it has to be checkable from the
outside. This page names, for every boundary where data crosses from one
party to another, the threats in each STRIDE category (**S**poofing,
**T**ampering, **R**epudiation, **I**nformation disclosure, **D**enial of
service, **E**levation of privilege), what stops them, and what is left.
Each defence points to the code or test that holds it; a row without one
is a known gap.

## What is protected

- **Notes and attachments** — the vault (browser storage, a folder, the
  phone).
- **Secrets** — AI keys, Git and cloud tokens, room passwords
  ([Secrets and encryption](/security/vault/)).
- **What the user types into AI** — prompts and the notes sent with them.
- **The app itself** — the code a user runs must be the code that was
  released ([Supply chain](/security/supply-chain/)).

## Who we defend against

| Attacker | Can | Cannot (assumed) |
|---|---|---|
| A malicious note or file (shared, imported, clipped, synced) | Put any bytes in a note, a `.canvas`, a front-matter block, a link | Run code outside the sandboxes |
| A network attacker / a relay or signaling server | Read and change traffic it carries | Break TLS or AES-GCM |
| A cloud provider (Dropbox, Drive, Gist) | Read, change, delete or hold back the files it stores | — |
| A plugin or live block | Run its own code in its sandbox | Reach the page's origin, the vault or the network without a granted capability |
| A cloud AI provider (only when the user chose one) | See what is sent to it | See anything under policy `local-only` |

| | Threat | Defence | Where |

| T | A path from a note, a zip or git leaves the vault (`../`) | Every path checked: no `.`/`..`/NUL segments; Rust checks the folder again | `src/storage/vault`, `src-tauri/vault` tests |

| | Threat | Defence | Where |

pages.title: Trusted repositories
pages.description: Let agents propose changes in a git repository you own without the extra outside-content question.
pages.md:
Notes that come from a **git clone or pull** are *outside content*:
someone else may have written them, and they may hide instructions for
an agent (see [Local agents → Outside content](/ai/local-agents/#outside-content-prompt-injection)).
So when an agent has read such a note, every change it proposes asks you
first, before it is even staged.

For a repository that is yours, such as your own notes repo or a repo
only your team pushes to, that question gets in the way. **Trust this
repo** turns it off for that repository.

## Turn it on

1. Open the command palette (⌘K) and run **Trusted repositories…**
   (group *Security*).
2. Every repository cloned in this browser is listed with a switch. All
   of them start as **Asks first**.
3. Turn the switch on and confirm. The repository is now **Trusted**.

The setting is saved **on this device only**. It is not synced, not
written into the repository, and not shared with collaborators.

## What changes

With the switch on, when everything outside in an agent's run comes from
trusted repositories:

- a change the agent proposes is **staged without the extra question**;
- the change still **waits for your review** in the staged changes list.
  Nothing is written until you apply it.

## What stays the same

- The repository's notes are still **delimited and cleaned** in the
  prompt, and the run still records that it read outside content.
- **Web requests still ask** (fetch a page, search the web): that is how
  text planted in a note could send your data out.
- Anything else outside in the same run asks as before: a clipped page,
  an imported folder, a web result, another repository that is not
  trusted, or a note in the trusted repository whose frontmatter says
  `untrusted: true`.

## When trust is dropped

Trust belongs to the repository you looked at, so it is removed when:

- you **clone again** into the same folder;
- you **rename or move** the repository folder, or move another folder
  onto its name.

Moving notes *inside* a trusted repository keeps it trusted. Turn the
switch off at any time to make agents ask again.

## Who should not use it

Anyone who can push to the repository can put text in front of your
agents. Do not trust a repository with outside contributors, a fork of
someone else's project, or a repository whose push access you don't
control.

pages.title: Usage on this device
pages.description: Lumen counts starts, commands and errors on your device only. The weekly report is off until you turn it on, and you send it yourself. Nothing leaves without your click.
pages.md:
Lumen has no analytics and no tracking. To know whether the app is used and
what breaks, it keeps a few **counters on your device**. They never leave
it unless you send them yourself.

## What is counted

Per day, in the browser's local storage (`lumen.usage.v1`):

| Counter | What it holds |
|---|---|
| Starts | how many times the app opened |
| Commands | how many times each command ran, by its id from the app's code (`file.exportHtml`, `help.feedback` …) |
| Errors | how many uncaught errors happened: one number, no message, no stack, no file |

The counters hold no note text, no file names, no user or device id and no
time of day. A counter name has to look like a command id: no spaces, no
slashes, no runs of digits or capitals. Anything you typed can't become one.
The last 60 days are kept.

## The dashboard

**Help: Usage on this device** in the command palette shows:

- the day you started using Lumen
- how many of the last 7 and 30 days you used it
- whether you came back after a week and after a month
- the most used commands, and how many commands went unused for 30 days

There you can turn counting off, which also clears the counts, or clear them
at any time.

## The weekly report: only when you send it

The dialog shows the whole report as JSON, exactly as it would be sent. It
holds counts only: the app version, the week, days used, retention, starts,
errors, the 20 most used commands of the app, and the number of unused ones.

- **Open on GitHub** opens a new tab with a GitHub issue form that has the
  report in it. Nothing is sent until you submit that form yourself. The
  click is listed in the [privacy ledger](/ai/privacy/) with its size.
- **Copy** puts the JSON on the clipboard.
- **Remind me once a week** is off by default. When you turn it on, a
  notice appears once a week with a button that opens the dialog. The notice
  sends nothing.

Without one of these clicks, Lumen makes no request for usage. The tests
check this (`src/__tests__/usageMetrics.test.ts`): counting, errors, the
dashboard and the report make 0 requests and add 0 ledger entries. A report
built after secrets were planted in the vault's storage contains none of
them.

pages.title: Vault encryption at rest
pages.description: Encrypt the whole vault where it is stored — OPFS, a real folder or the desktop folder — with a passphrase, a recovery key and auto-lock.
pages.md:
Optional. **Command palette → Vault encryption…** encrypts every note and
file of the vault where it is stored, so a copied browser profile, a lost
laptop or a synced folder shows only ciphertext. Lumen asks for the
passphrase when it opens the vault.

> **Read this before you turn it on.** An encrypted vault can't be read as
> plain text by Obsidian, git, a text editor or any other program — only by
> Lumen with the passphrase or the recovery key. If you use the same folder
> with other tools, keep the vault unencrypted (or keep a plain export).

## What is encrypted

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| Every file of the vault — notes, attachments, canvases, `.trash/`, `.git/` | AES-256-GCM, one random nonce per write, on every storage: the browser's own storage (OPFS), a real folder you picked in the browser, the desktop app's folder |
| History snapshots (the backups the Version History panel shows) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB |
| Agent traces (the last 50 runs, which include parts of notes) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB; migrated when encryption is turned on, deleted when it is turned off |
| Semantic search index (embeddings and the text of each chunk) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB |
| AI answer cache | Not written while the vault is encrypted; emptied when encryption is turned on or off |
| The open note and the open tabs, which Lumen normally keeps in `localStorage` to resume a session | Not kept; after a reload you open the notes again from the vault |

The fast search index lives in memory only and is never stored.

**Not encrypted:** file and folder names, file sizes and dates (the vault
stays a normal folder of files); the list of recent files; API keys and
tokens (they have their own store, see [Secrets and encryption](/security/vault/));
the encrypted sync's own state; version history of live collaboration rooms;
results of batch AI jobs; what the learning critic remembers. A vault export
(zip or folder) is plain text on purpose.

## Passphrase, recovery key, lock

- **Passphrase** — at least 12 characters. The key is derived with
  PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 iterations (the same function as the
  [encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/)). Argon2id is reserved in the format and
  replaces it once its library is added; a vault that asks for Argon2id is
  refused by an older Lumen, never misread.
- **Recovery key** — 30 characters (150 random bits), shown **once**, when
  you turn encryption on, before anything is encrypted. Lumen goes on only
  after you confirm you saved it. The vault's key is derived from it, so it
  opens the vault even if you forget the passphrase *and* even if the
  vault's encryption header files were lost. Case, spaces and dashes don't
  matter when you type it back.
- **Lock** — after 15 minutes without a key press or a click (choose 5, 15,
  30, 60 minutes or never in the dialog), or **Lock now**. A locked vault
  covers the app with the unlock screen; nothing is read or written until it
  is unlocked, and saves made meanwhile go on afterwards.
- **Change passphrase** re-wraps the key; no file is re-encrypted.

## Safety: what happens if something goes wrong

- **Wrong passphrase** — refused; nothing is read or written.
- **Turning it on or off is cut off** (tab closed, battery, crash) — each
  file is converted copy-first: the new version is written next to it,
  read back and checked, and only then replaces the file. Every file is
  always either complete plain text or complete ciphertext, and Lumen reads
  both. **Check and repair** finishes the job.
- **A file changed by another program meanwhile** is left alone and done by
  the next run. A file that doesn't decrypt with this vault's key is
  reported and never overwritten or deleted.
- **The header** (`.lumen-encryption.json`, plus `.lumen-encryption.backup.json`)
  is written twice; one damaged copy is fine. It is removed only when no
  encrypted file is left. If both are gone, the recovery key brings the
  vault back.
- **A plain file dropped into the folder** reads normally and is encrypted
  by Check and repair.
- An encrypted vault can't be **moved** to another place (the move would
  copy decrypted notes): turn encryption off, move, turn it on again.

## Turning it off

**Vault encryption… → Turn off encryption** asks for the passphrase again,
then decrypts every file back to plain text. History comes back in the clear;
agent traces and the semantic index are deleted (they are rebuilt).

If both are gone, the recovery key brings the vault back. A plain file dropped into the folder reads normally and is encrypted by Check and repair. An encrypted vault can't be moved to another place (the move would copy decrypted notes): turn encryption off, move, turn it on again.

pages.title: Secrets and encryption
pages.description: How Lumen stores API keys and tokens, and how to encrypt a document.
pages.md:
Lumen keeps the secrets it needs — AI provider keys, Git and cloud tokens,
the collaboration room password, the research search key — out of plain
browser storage. The whole vault can also be encrypted with a passphrase and
a recovery key — see [Vault encryption at rest](/security/vault-encryption/);
the secrets described here are kept apart from it.

## Where secrets live

| Where Lumen runs | How secrets are stored |
|---|---|
| Browser / installed web app | Each secret is encrypted with AES-GCM-256 under a WebCrypto key that is **non-extractable**: no script can read out the raw key bytes. The secrets no longer sit in localStorage as plain text, so a glance in DevTools, a localStorage dump or a synced settings export shows only ciphertext. |
| Desktop app on macOS / Windows | The operating system's keychain (Keychain / Credential Manager). Lumen keeps only the secret names, so it knows what to load. |
| Old engines without IndexedDB or WebCrypto | Plain localStorage, as before. Lumen reports this mode instead of hiding it. |

**Honest limits:**

- The key is stored in the same IndexedDB database as the encrypted
  secrets, and Lumen decrypts them at startup without asking for a
  password. Someone who copies the whole browser profile and opens it in
  Lumen can therefore use the stored key and read the secrets.
  Non-extractable stops the key from being *exported*, not from being
  *used*. Protecting against a copied profile needs a password you type
  (planned with whole-vault encryption, task 11.4) or the desktop app's
  OS keychain.
- Code running inside Lumen's own origin could also ask WebCrypto to
  decrypt. The Content Security Policy and the HTML sanitizer are what
  keep foreign code out.

Plain-text secrets left by older versions are encrypted and moved at startup.

## Encrypting a document

`⌘K → 🔒 Encrypt Document` encrypts the open note with AES-256-GCM under a
password you type. The note is replaced by an encrypted block; `Decrypt
Document` restores it. Lumen does not keep the password — lose it and the
note cannot be recovered.

## What is not encrypted

Your notes themselves are plain Markdown files (in the browser's private
file system, or a folder on desktop). Encrypting the whole vault at rest is
planned as an option (plan task 11.4).
